content: Juniperus virginiana, commonly known as Eastern Juniper or Eastern Red Cedar, is a species of juniper native to North America. Despite its common name, it is not closely related to true cedars of the genus Cedrus. Among the Lakota Native Americans, it is referred to as Chansha, meaning redwood, or Hante'. This tree is distributed from southeastern Canada to the Gulf of Mexico, primarily east of the Great Plains. In regions further west, it is replaced by Juniperus scopulorum (Rocky Mountain Juniper), and in the southwest, by Juniperus ashei (Ashe Juniper). Eastern Juniper is a dense, slow-growing tree that may remain a shrub on poor soils but typically grows to heights of 5–18 meters (16–59 feet), occasionally reaching 25 meters (82 feet). Its trunk diameter is usually 30–60 cm (1–2 feet), though it can rarely reach up to 120 cm (4 feet). The largest specimens, found in bottomlands of southeastern U.S. states, can live up to 300 years. The bark is reddish-brown, fibrous, and peels off in narrow strips. The leaves of Juniperus virginiana are of two types: sharp, needle-like juvenile leaves measuring 5–10 mm in length, and tightly pressed, scale-like adult leaves measuring 2–4 mm in length. Juvenile leaves are present on young plants up to 1–3 years old and as scattered shoots on adult trees, particularly in shaded areas. The cones are berry-like, 3–7 mm long, with fleshy scales. They are dark purple-blue with a white waxy coating, giving them a sky-blue appearance, although the wax often rubs off. These cones mature in 6–8 months and serve as a winter food source for many bird species, which help disperse the wingless seeds. Eastern Juniper is a host for apple rust disease and is considered a pioneer species, meaning it is one of the first trees to colonize cleared, eroded, or otherwise damaged land. It is often found along highways, near construction sites, in prairies, oak barrens, old pastures, and limestone hills. There are two recognized subspecies of Juniperus virginiana, which intergrade where their ranges overlap: 1. Juniperus virginiana subsp. virginiana: Known as Eastern Juniper or Red Cedar, this subspecies is found in eastern North America, from Maine west to southern Ontario and South Dakota, and south to northern Florida and east-central Texas. Its cones are larger (4–7 mm), its scale leaves are acute at the apex, and its bark is red-brown. 2. Juniperus virginiana subsp. silicicola: Known as Southern or Sand Juniper/Red Cedar, this subspecies is found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts from North Carolina south to central Florida and west to southeast Texas. Its cones are smaller (3–4 mm), its scale leaves are blunt at the apex, and its bark is orange-brown. Some authors treat this subspecies as a distinct species, while others classify it as a variety. Uses The heartwood of Juniperus virginiana is fine-grained, soft, brittle, and ranges in color from pinkish-red to brownish-red. It is fragrant, lightweight, and highly durable, even in contact with soil. When properly prepared, it is an excellent material for crafting English-style longbows, flatbows, and Native American sinewed bows. Historically, it was a premier wood for pencil production. Its natural resistance to rot and its ability to repel moths make it a popular choice for lining clothes chests and closets, often referred to as cedar closets or cedar chests. This same rot resistance makes it suitable for use as fence posts. The wood is marketed as eastern red cedar or aromatic cedar. Juniper oil is distilled from the wood, twigs, and leaves of the tree. The cones are used to flavor gin and have been employed as a kidney medicine. Native American tribes historically used juniper wood poles to demarcate tribal hunting territories. French traders named Baton Rouge, Louisiana (red stick), after the reddish color of these poles. During the Dust Bowl drought of the 1930s, the Prairie States Forestry Project encouraged farmers to plant shelterbelts (windbreaks) of Eastern Juniper across the Great Plains. While still used for this purpose, the tree is now considered invasive in many areas, even within its native range. Previously controlled by periodic wildfires, unchecked growth of Eastern Juniper can be destructive to grasslands. Efforts to manage its spread include cutting and prescribed burning. The trees are highly flammable, and dense populations were implicated in the rapid spread of wildfires in drought-stricken Oklahoma and Texas in 2005 and 2006. In the Missouri and Arkansas Ozarks, Eastern Junipers (locally called cedars) are commonly used as Christmas trees. Allergen Information The pollen of Eastern Juniper is a known allergen, though it is less potent than that of the related Juniperus ashei (Ashe Juniper), which releases pollen about a month earlier. Individuals allergic to one species are often allergic to both. Eastern Juniper sheds pollen from late winter through early spring, meaning that allergies triggered by Ashe Juniper in winter may extend into spring due to the subsequent pollination of Eastern Juniper. Additionally, contact with the leaves or wood of Eastern Juniper can cause mild skin irritation in some individuals.
